The biggest mistake first-time buyers make? They buy with their emotions and justify it with logic after.

They fall in love with the kitchen. The backyard. The street. And then every decision gets made to protect that feeling. Waiving conditions they should keep. Stretching the budget past what's comfortable. Ignoring what their gut was already telling them.

I've watched buyers talk themselves into offers they knew were wrong because they couldn't stand the idea of losing the house.

Here's what I tell every first-time buyer I work with. The right house doesn't require you to talk yourself into it. And if the deal only works if everything goes perfectly, it's not the right deal.

Your first home is your biggest investment. Make that decision like one.
I'm Tristian Clunis with Royal LePage. Buying in Durham and want someone in your corner? Let's talk.

Month three: you start a list of things you want to fix. The list gets long fast.

None of this means buying was wrong. It means buying unprepared is hard.

The people who do best walked in with realistic expectations, a real budget, and an emergency fund. That's what I try to give every client before closing day. Not just excitement. Preparation.

Not every deal makes it to closing. Nobody talks about why.

Financing falls through. Pre-approved, went firm, then something changed. New credit card, missed payment, job loss. Lender pulls back. Deal dead.

Inspection blowups. Something unexpected comes up and neither side will move on who pays for it.

Buyer panic. This one is real. The doubt that sets in between accepted offer and closing, especially for first-timers.

And here's what most people don't know. In Ontario, walking away after you've gone firm isn't just losing your deposit. The seller can come after you for more. I have that conversation with every client before we write anything.

Appraisal gaps. In a bidding war the lender sometimes appraises below the purchase price. Now there's a shortfall the buyer has to cover in cash or renegotiate.

Most of these are preventable with the right preparation and the right people around you.

Most people spend more time researching a TV than choosing their real estate agent. Here are the questions you should actually be asking.

How many homes have you sold in the last 12 months and where? An agent who mostly works in Mississauga doesn't know Durham. Specificity matters.

What does your marketing actually include? If the answer is MLS and social media and they stop there, that's not a plan.

How do you handle multiple offers? Strategy or gut feeling?

Can I see a sample of your recent listings? Photos, description, presentation. That tells you everything.

What happens if I'm not happy? Is there an easy exit clause or are you locked in?

A confident agent welcomes every one of these. A weak one gets defensive.

Most buyers still don't fully understand how a buyer's agent gets paid. And it costs some of them the biggest decision of their life.

In Ontario, the seller typically covers the buyer's agent commission. That's been the standard for decades and it still applies in most transactions. That said, since recent rule changes, buyers now sign a representation agreement upfront that spells out exactly how their agent gets paid. In the vast majority of deals, that cost still doesn't come out of your pocket. But you deserve to know how it works before you sign anything.

Here's what that representation actually gets you. Comps pulled before every offer so you know what the home is worth. Problems flagged that you'd never catch on your own. Negotiation on price, conditions, closing date, and inclusions. And someone in your corner when things go sideways.

First-time buyers in Ontario are leaving real money on the table. Most don't even know these programs exist.

Land Transfer Tax Rebate: up to $4,000 back on closing day.

RRSP Home Buyers' Plan: withdraw up to $35,000 tax-free for your down payment. Couples can pull $70,000 combined and have 15 years to repay it.

First Home Savings Account: $8,000 a year, tax deductible going in and tax-free coming out. If you haven't opened one yet, open one today. Every year you wait is $8,000 you can't go back and contribute.

GST/HST New Build Rebate: buying new construction? You may qualify for a partial rebate on the HST you paid.

Combined these programs can put $10,000 to $70,000 back in your pocket. Talk to your agent and mortgage broker before you assume you know what you qualify for.

Here's how I can tell if a house is overpriced in under 60 seconds.

Days on market. If it's been sitting 30, 40, 50 days in a moving market, something is wrong. Usually the price.

Price changes. Open the listing history. One or two reductions means the seller started too high and is chasing the market down.

Recent sales. Pull three comparable homes that sold in the last 60 to 90 days. Same beds, same neighbourhood, similar condition. If this listing is 10% above that number it's overpriced.

Buyer activity. Is it quiet? Are agents saying nobody is coming back for second showings? Silence is data.

You don't need years of experience to spot an overpriced home. You need comps and patience. I bring both to every client I work with.

Whitby is the sweet spot. Strong resale, good schools, family-friendly neighbourhoods, and still more accessible than Pickering or Toronto.

Oshawa gives you the most house for your money. Full stop. If budget is driving the decision and you're okay going a little further east, Oshawa wins on square footage every time.

Condo vs Freehold. Here's what actually matters.

The condo fee isn't the enemy. If it's $600 a month and it covers building insurance, exterior maintenance, and the reserve fund, that's real money you're not spending out of pocket. A freehold owner pays all of that too, just in unpredictable chunks.

The real question is lifestyle and control. In a condo, decisions about the building aren't yours. In a freehold, you do whatever you want but you also own every problem.

For first-time buyers, condos often make more sense as an entry point. For families, freehold wins on space and flexibility.

Neither is wrong. Buying the wrong one for your situation is.

Everyone assumes a brand new home is the safe choice. Here's what builders don't tell you before you sign.

New builds look clean and fresh with zero problems. But you're paying today's price for a home you won't move into for 12 to 24 months. A lot can change in that window.

The closing costs on a new build are brutal. Development charges, Tarion fees, HST that isn't always fully rebated, utility hookups, landscaping. Resale you see exactly what you're getting. You move in on a real date. What you negotiate is what you pay.

New builds aren't wrong. They're just not the safe, simple choice people think they are. Read the agreement. Hire a lawyer who knows builder contracts. And know your actual number before you sign anything.

You can't time the market perfectly. But you can know when you have more leverage.
Spring means more listings and more competition. Bidding wars, pressure, and a lot of buyers fighting for the same good ones.

Summer slows down. Families are away. Serious sellers are still listing but fewer buyers are out. That's leverage.

Fall brings motivated sellers back. If something didn't sell in spring, by October that seller is ready to deal.

Winter is the hidden gem. Sellers listing in December and January need to move. Low inventory but low competition, and motivated sellers negotiate.

The worst time to buy is when everyone else is buying. The best time is when you're financially ready and emotionally prepared, regardless of the season.

The number your bank approves you for and the number you should actually spend are not the same number.

Banks qualify you on gross income. They don't account for daycare, car payments, groceries, or your actual life. They'll approve you for the max — and then you have to live inside that payment every single month.

Real example. $150K household income in Ontario qualifies for roughly $650K to $750K right now. The monthly payment on $700K at current rates is $4,100 to $4,500. Add Durham property tax ($500 to $600/month), utilities, and maintenance.
You're looking at $5,500 to $6,000 a month in housing. On $150K gross your take-home is around $9,500 to $10,000.

That's over half your income. The bank said yes. But does that number work for your life?

This is the conversation I have with every buyer before we look at a single house.

14 years walking through Durham & GTA homes. Here are the red flags I spot immediately.

Horizontal foundation cracks. Not cosmetic. That's a structural conversation.

Old electrical. Knob and tube or aluminum wiring. Most insurers won't touch it and replacing it isn't cheap.

Water stains anywhere. Ceiling, basement walls, around windows. Water gets in and slowly destroys everything around it.

Fresh drywall patch in a weird spot. New paint only in the basement. That's someone covering something up.

Soft floors near bathrooms or kitchens. Water damage under the surface.
None of this shows up in the listing photos. That's why the walkthrough matters and why having the right person in that room with you changes everything.

caption:
Selling "over asking" doesn't mean someone got a deal. Most of the time it means the opposite.

Here's how it actually works. An agent lists a home $100K below market on purpose. It gets 20 showings in a weekend. Buyers get emotional. They overbid. The house sells $80K "over asking" — exactly as planned.

The number that matters isn't list price vs sale price. It's sale price vs the actual comps.

If two identical homes sold for $850K last month and this one sold for $920K "over asking" — that buyer didn't win. They overpaid.

Pull the comps before you write anything. I do this for every client before we ever step into a bidding war.
